sprints.title: Repo Scout — GitHub API scraper for cybersecurity education repos
sprints.notes: Build the primary GitHub scraper using the GitHub Search API. Search strategies: (1) Topic-based search — query repos tagged with: cybersecurity, ethical-hacking, infosec, penetration-testing, ctf, network-security, cloud-security, malware-analysis, digital-forensics, incident-response, oscp, ceh, comptia, security-plus, ccna, sysadmin, linux-administration, windows-server. (2) Keyword search — search repo names and descriptions for: 'course', 'curriculum', 'slides', 'lecture', 'lab', 'workshop', 'bootcamp', 'training', 'educational', 'learning-path', 'study-guide', 'certification', 'exam-prep'. (3) Awesome-list mining — scrape awesome-cybersecurity, awesome-hacking, awesome-pentest, awesome-security, awesome-infosec and similar curated lists for linked repos. (4) Organization scanning — scan known edu orgs: OWASP, SANS, NIST repos, university CS departments with public course materials. (5) User-based — find prolific cybersecurity educators on GitHub and scan their repos. Filters: minimum 10 stars, has license file, last updated within 2 years, contains markdown/HTML/PDF/PPTX content (not just code tools). Output: per-repo JSON record with metadata, content preview, and Hexworth house recommendation. CLI: node _tools/repo-scout/scout.js scan --topic cybersecurity --min-stars 10.

sprints.title: Repo Scout — GitLab and alternative platform scrapers
sprints.notes: Extend Repo Scout beyond GitHub to other platforms. GitLab: use GitLab API (v4) to search public projects with cybersecurity/education topics. Many university courses host on GitLab (self-hosted instances and gitlab.com). Bitbucket: search public repos — less common for edu content but some exist. SourceHut: niche but growing, some security research hosted here. Academic sources: (1) MIT OpenCourseWare — scrape course listings for computer science and cybersecurity, find linked GitHub repos or downloadable materials. (2) Coursera/edX — identify open-source companion repos for security courses. (3) Open Textbook Library — search for CC-licensed cybersecurity and networking textbooks. (4) Archive.org — search for archived educational materials with permissive licenses. Non-repo content sources: (5) SlideShare/SpeakerDeck — scrape for cybersecurity presentation decks with CC licenses. (6) NIST/CISA public resources — training materials, frameworks, guides (all public domain). Each platform gets its own scraper module under _tools/repo-scout/scrapers/. Common output format so all discoveries feed into the same manifest.

sprints.title: Repo Scout — Content classifier and house mapper
sprints.notes: Build an automated classifier that analyzes discovered repos and maps them to Hexworth houses. Analysis steps: (1) File type inventory — count markdown, HTML, PPTX, PDF, Jupyter notebooks, YAML, code files to determine content type (lecture slides, labs, reference docs, tools). (2) Keyword extraction — scan README and top-level docs for domain keywords: map to houses using keyword → house lookup table (e.g., 'firewall' → shield/web, 'malware' → dark-arts, 'AWS' → cloud, 'subnet' → web, 'Arduino' → forge, 'Python' → code, 'cryptography' → key, 'SIEM' → eye, 'PowerShell' → script). (3) License classifier — categorize license permissiveness (Public Domain > CC0 > MIT > Apache 2.0 > CC-BY > CC-BY-SA > GPL > CC-BY-NC > proprietary/unknown). Flag non-commercial licenses as 'review required'. (4) Quality scoring — composite score based on: stars, forks, recency, content volume, file organization, README quality, license permissiveness. (5) Conversion effort estimator — small (< 10 files, simple markdown), medium (10-50 files, mixed formats), large (50+ files or complex PPTX/PDF conversion). Output: enriched discovery record with house[], contentType, license, qualityScore, conversionEffort, recommended priority. CLI: node _tools/repo-scout/scout.js classify --input discoveries.json.

sprints.title: Repo Scout — Discovery dashboard and review workflow
sprints.notes: Build a dashboard to review, approve, and track discovered repos. Features: (1) Discovery browser — filterable/sortable table of all discovered repos: name, URL, house mapping, quality score, license, conversion effort, status (new/reviewed/approved/forked/converting/converted/rejected). (2) Review workflow — click a discovery to see full details: README preview, file tree, content samples, license text, similar repos already in pipeline. Mark as 'approve for fork', 'reject' (with reason), or 'bookmark for later'. (3) Fork tracker — once approved, track the fork process: forked → content extracted → conversion sprint created → conversion in progress → integrated into Prime. (4) Stats dashboard — total discoveries, by house, by license, by status, conversion pipeline metrics. (5) Scheduled scanning — configure cron/scheduled task to run scrapers weekly and surface new discoveries. (6) Duplicate detection — flag repos that contain substantially similar content to already-forked repos or existing Prime content. Build as HTML page in _tools/repo-scout/dashboard.html or as CLI reports: node _tools/repo-scout/scout.js dashboard, node _tools/repo-scout/scout.js report --format md.

sprints.title: Repo Scout — Auto-fork and content extraction pipeline
sprints.notes: Automate the fork → extract → stage pipeline. Auto-fork: use GitHub API (or gh CLI) to fork approved repos to the FM-256 GitHub organization. Naming convention: hexworth-source-{original-repo-name}. Content extraction: (1) Clone the forked repo locally to _planning/repo-scout-imports/{repo-name}/. (2) Extract convertible content — PPTX files (use python-pptx to extract text + images), PDF files (extract text with PyMuPDF/pdfplumber), Markdown files (copy directly), Jupyter notebooks (extract cells), HTML slides (copy directly). (3) Generate a conversion manifest: source file → target Prime file mapping, with house assignment and module numbering. (4) Auto-create sprint items — for each repo, generate EHE-style sprint items in sprints.json for the conversion work (one item per module/chapter). Safeguards: never auto-fork without approval flag, never overwrite existing Prime content, always preserve attribution and license in extracted content. CLI: node _tools/repo-scout/scout.js fork RS-{id}, node _tools/repo-scout/scout.js extract {repo-name}.

sprints.title: Repo Scout — License compliance and attribution tracker
sprints.notes: Build a license compliance system to ensure all forked and converted content respects original licenses. Components: (1) License database — for every forked repo, store: original license text, license type (SPDX identifier), original author(s), original URL, fork date, any license conditions (attribution required, share-alike, non-commercial). (2) Attribution generator — automatically generate attribution notices for converted content. Each Prime module converted from external source gets a footer or metadata field: 'Adapted from [Original Title] by [Author], licensed under [License]. Original: [URL]'. (3) License compatibility matrix — which licenses allow what: can we modify? must we share-alike? can we use commercially? must we attribute? (4) Compliance checker — scan _planning/repo-scout-imports/ and cross-reference with license database, flag any content lacking license info or using incompatible licenses. (5) NOTICE file — maintain a master NOTICE.md listing all third-party content sources, licenses, and attribution. This is non-negotiable — protects Hexworth legally and respects open-source community. Store at _tools/repo-scout/licenses.json and generate NOTICE.md.

sprints.title: Repo Scout — Conversion template engine for common formats
sprints.notes: Build reusable conversion templates to speed up the raw-to-Prime pipeline. Templates needed: (1) PPTX → Presentation HTML — extract slides from PowerPoint, convert to Prime slide-based presentation format with correct house theme (auto-detect house from RS-4 classification). Handle: text extraction, bullet points, images (export to assets/), tables, code blocks, speaker notes. (2) Markdown → Presentation HTML — convert structured markdown (headings = slides) to Prime presentation format. (3) PDF → Presentation HTML — extract pages/sections, OCR if scanned, convert to slides. (4) Jupyter Notebook → Lab HTML — convert notebook cells to Prime interactive lab format. (5) Quiz/Test Bank → Quiz HTML — parse common test bank formats (CSV, QTI, Respondus, plain text Q&A) into Prime quiz format. Each template: auto-applies correct house color palette, adds Hexworth navigation chrome, generates content-registry.js entry stub, creates progress tracking hooks. CLI: node _tools/repo-scout/convert.js --input source.pptx --house dark-arts --module-id ehe-01 --type presentation. This is the force multiplier — makes bulk conversion feasible instead of hand-building every module.

sprints.title: Repo Scout — Initial seed scan and first batch fork
sprints.notes: Run the first production scan and fork the initial batch of high-value repos. Target: 50-100 discovered repos, fork top 10-20 highest-quality finds. Priority search targets by house: Dark Arts (ethical hacking courses, CTF writeup collections, pentest methodology repos), Web (networking courses, CCNA/Network+ study materials, protocol labs), Cloud (AWS/Azure/GCP security courses, cloud architecture materials), Code (programming courses with security focus, algorithm visualizations), Shield (GRC frameworks, compliance guides, risk assessment templates), Key (cryptography courses, crypto challenge sets), Eye (SIEM/SOC training materials, log analysis courses, threat hunting playbooks), Script (automation courses, scripting tutorials, DevOps security), Forge (hardware hacking, IoT security, embedded systems courses). Deliverable: first discoveries.json populated, first batch of forks completed, conversion sprints auto-generated for top 5 repos. This proves the pipeline end-to-end and starts feeding fresh content into the conversion queue.

sprints.title: Neon Server — Hardware inventory, drive assessment, and BIOS/UEFI setup
sprints.notes: Physical setup and inventory of the Neon main server. Tasks: (1) Document hardware specs — CPU, RAM (total and configuration), motherboard model, NIC(s), GPU if any, PSU wattage. (2) Inventory all hard drives — make, model, capacity, interface (SATA, NVMe, SAS), current health (SMART data), RPM/type (HDD vs SSD). (3) Decide drive layout strategy: which drive(s) for OS, which for data/databases, which for backups, any hot spares. (4) BIOS/UEFI configuration — boot order, enable virtualization (VT-x/AMD-V, VT-d/IOMMU if needed), AHCI mode for SATA, NVMe configuration, fan/thermal settings, wake-on-LAN if desired. (5) Check/update firmware — BIOS, drive firmware, NIC firmware, RAID controller firmware if applicable. (6) Physical setup — rack/shelf placement, power connections (UPS if available), network cabling (at least 1 Gbps, ideally 2.5/10G if hardware supports), KVM or remote management (IPMI/iLO/iDRAC if server-grade). Deliverable: hardware manifest document and drive layout plan approved before OS install.

sprints.title: Neon Server — OS installation and base system configuration
sprints.notes: Install and configure the base operating system on Neon. Decisions: (1) OS selection — Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS (stable, wide support, 5-year maintenance), Debian 12 (rock-solid, minimal), Rocky Linux 9 / AlmaLinux 9 (RHEL-based, enterprise), or Proxmox VE (if running VMs/containers as primary workload). (2) Disk partitioning — recommended layout: boot partition (1GB, ext4), root partition (50-100GB SSD, ext4/xfs), swap (1-2x RAM or 8GB cap), /home (SSD, user data), /var (separate partition for logs/databases, SSD), /data (large HDD pool for bulk storage — mounted separately). Consider LVM for flexible resizing. (3) RAID configuration — if multiple drives: RAID 1 for OS (mirror for redundancy), RAID 5/6 or ZFS raidz1/raidz2 for data pool (capacity with parity), or ZFS mirror pairs. ZFS preferred if RAM allows (1GB per TB of storage). (4) Base config — hostname (neon), static IP on LAN, SSH server (key-only auth, disable password auth, non-standard port optional), firewall (ufw or firewalld — deny all, allow SSH), timezone, NTP sync, automatic security updates (unattended-upgrades). (5) User setup — admin user, sudo group, SSH key deployment from dev machines.

sprints.title: Neon Server — Storage pool setup and mount strategy
sprints.notes: Configure storage pools and mount points for organized data management. Tasks: (1) Create storage pools — if using ZFS: create zpools (tank, fast-pool for SSDs, bulk-pool for HDDs), set compression (lz4), set atime=off, create datasets for each purpose. If using LVM: create volume groups and logical volumes. If using mdadm RAID: create arrays, format, mount. (2) Mount point structure: /data/hexworth/ (Hexworth project repos and working copies), /data/databases/ (database data directories), /data/backups/ (automated backup target), /data/media/ (raw source content — PPTX, PDF, videos), /data/repos/ (forked GitHub repos from Repo Scout), /data/scratch/ (temp workspace for conversions). (3) Permissions — create hexworth group, set proper ownership and permissions on each mount point, ACLs if needed for multi-user access. (4) fstab entries — ensure all mounts persist across reboots with correct options (noatime, nofail for non-critical). (5) Monitoring — set up disk space alerts (df thresholds), SMART monitoring (smartmontools + smartd for drive health alerts), ZFS scrub schedule if using ZFS (monthly). (6) Network shares — Samba share for Windows access from dev machines, NFS for Linux clients, or both. Ensure Hexworth project data is accessible from the WSL development environment.

sprints.title: Neon Server — Database server installation (PostgreSQL + MongoDB)
sprints.notes: Install and configure database servers on Neon. PostgreSQL (relational): (1) Install PostgreSQL 16 (latest stable). (2) Configure postgresql.conf — listen_addresses (LAN IP or 0.0.0.0), port 5432, shared_buffers (25% of RAM), effective_cache_size (75% of RAM), work_mem, maintenance_work_mem, WAL settings for durability. (3) Configure pg_hba.conf — local auth (peer/md5), LAN access (md5/scram-sha-256, restrict to subnet). (4) Create databases: hexworth_prime (Prime platform data), hexworth_arena (Arena game data), hexworth_colosseum (Colosseum game data), hexworth_analytics (usage analytics, progress tracking). (5) Create application user(s) with least-privilege roles. MongoDB (document store): (1) Install MongoDB 7.x Community. (2) Configure mongod.conf — bindIp (LAN), port 27017, storage.dbPath (/data/databases/mongodb), enable authentication. (3) Create databases: hexworth_content (content registry, course materials), hexworth_users (user profiles, progress). (4) Create application users with appropriate roles. Both: (5) Firewall rules — allow DB ports only from trusted LAN IPs. (6) Verify connectivity from dev machines. (7) Basic backup scripts (pg_dump, mongodump) running on cron to /data/backups/.

sprints.title: Neon Server — Network configuration and remote access
sprints.notes: Configure Neon's network for reliable LAN access and optional remote access. LAN setup: (1) Static IP assignment — either static in netplan/NetworkManager or DHCP reservation on router. (2) Hostname resolution — add neon to /etc/hosts on dev machines, or set up local DNS (Pi-hole, dnsmasq) so 'neon' or 'neon.local' resolves from all devices. (3) mDNS/Avahi — install avahi-daemon so neon.local works via mDNS (zero-config). (4) Firewall rules — allow: SSH (22 or custom), PostgreSQL (5432), MongoDB (27017), Samba (445), NFS (2049), HTTP/HTTPS (80/443 for future web services), monitoring (9090 Prometheus, 3000 Grafana). Deny all else. Remote access (optional): (5) Tailscale or WireGuard VPN — secure tunnel for accessing Neon from outside LAN without exposing ports to internet. Tailscale is zero-config; WireGuard is lighter but manual. (6) SSH jump host — if no VPN, SSH on non-standard port with fail2ban for brute-force protection. (7) Dynamic DNS — if ISP gives dynamic IP, set up DDNS (DuckDNS, Cloudflare, No-IP) for consistent remote hostname. (8) Speed test — verify network throughput between dev machines and Neon (iperf3).

sprints.title: Neon Server — Docker and container runtime setup
sprints.notes: Install Docker and container infrastructure on Neon for running services. Tasks: (1) Install Docker Engine (not Docker Desktop — server has no GUI). Add docker group, add admin user to docker group. (2) Install Docker Compose v2 (plugin). (3) Configure Docker — data-root on data drive (not OS drive), default logging driver (json-file with max-size/max-file rotation), DNS settings, default network. (4) Set up docker-compose project structure: /data/hexworth/docker/ with per-service compose files. (5) Initial containers to consider: Portainer (web UI for managing containers), Nginx Proxy Manager or Traefik (reverse proxy for web services), Watchtower (auto-update containers), Uptime Kuma (service monitoring). (6) Container networking — create hexworth-net bridge network for inter-container communication. (7) Volume strategy — named volumes stored on data drives, bind mounts for config files. (8) If databases end up containerized instead of bare-metal (NE-4), set up persistent volumes on data drives with proper backup hooks. Docker gives flexibility to spin up dev/staging environments, run Repo Scout scrapers in containers, or add services like Redis, Elasticsearch, or MinIO later without cluttering the base OS.

sprints.title: Neon Server — Backup strategy and disaster recovery
sprints.notes: Set up automated backups and a disaster recovery plan. Backup targets: (1) Databases — pg_dump (PostgreSQL) and mongodump (MongoDB) nightly to /data/backups/db/ with 7-day rotation. (2) Configuration — /etc/ configs, Docker compose files, cron jobs, firewall rules — backed up weekly. (3) Hexworth project data — git repos are self-backed-up to GitHub, but local working copies and non-git data (raw source content, converted assets, uploaded media) need backup. (4) Backup destination — local backup drive (separate physical drive from data drives), plus off-site: rsync to a cloud storage bucket (Backblaze B2 is cheapest at $5/TB/month), or rsync to a second machine. Tools: (5) restic or borg for deduplicated, encrypted, incremental backups. (6) Cron schedule: databases nightly, full system weekly, configs on change. (7) Backup verification — monthly test restore to confirm backups are valid (untested backups are not backups). (8) Disaster recovery runbook — document: how to rebuild Neon from scratch, where backups live, restore order (OS → storage → databases → services → data), estimated recovery time. Store runbook in the repo, not only on Neon.

sprints.title: Neon Server — Monitoring, alerting, and health dashboard
sprints.notes: Set up monitoring so you know when something goes wrong before it becomes a problem. Stack: (1) Prometheus (metrics collection) — node_exporter for system metrics (CPU, RAM, disk, network, temperature), postgres_exporter for PostgreSQL metrics, mongodb_exporter for MongoDB metrics. (2) Grafana (dashboards) — system overview dashboard (CPU, RAM, disk I/O, network throughput, temperatures), database dashboard (connections, query performance, cache hit ratio, replication lag), Docker dashboard (container status, resource usage), storage dashboard (pool usage, SMART health, ZFS scrub status). (3) Alerting — Grafana alerts or Alertmanager: disk space > 85%, CPU sustained > 90%, RAM > 90%, drive SMART warning, database connection failures, backup job failures, container crash/restart. Notification channels: email, Slack/Discord webhook, or Pushover for mobile push. (4) Uptime Kuma — simple uptime monitor for all services (HTTP endpoints, TCP ports, Docker containers), public status page optional. (5) Log aggregation (optional) — Loki + Promtail for centralized log searching, or simple logrotate + journald for basics. All monitoring services run as Docker containers (NE-6).

sprints.title: Neon Server — Security hardening and access control
sprints.notes: Harden Neon against attack — practice what Hexworth teaches. SSH hardening: (1) Key-only authentication (disable PasswordAuthentication), (2) disable root login, (3) AllowUsers whitelist, (4) fail2ban for brute-force protection (ban after 5 failed attempts, 1-hour ban). Firewall: (5) ufw/firewalld — default deny incoming, explicit allow per service, rate-limit SSH. System hardening: (6) Automatic security updates (unattended-upgrades on Ubuntu/Debian, dnf-automatic on RHEL-based). (7) Remove unnecessary services (telnet, FTP, avahi if not needed). (8) Disable unused network protocols (IPv6 if not used). (9) File integrity monitoring — AIDE or Tripwire for detecting unauthorized changes to system files. (10) AppArmor or SELinux — enforce mandatory access controls. (11) Kernel hardening — sysctl settings (disable IP forwarding unless routing, enable SYN cookies, disable ICMP redirects). (12) User audit — review /etc/passwd, no shared accounts, strong passwords for any non-key accounts. (13) Regular vulnerability scanning — run Lynis audit monthly, review findings. (14) Logging — ensure auditd is running for security event logging, forward logs to centralized location. This is Hexworth's own server — it should be a model of the security practices we teach.

sprints.title: Neon Server — Dev environment integration and workflow connection
sprints.notes: Connect Neon to the daily development workflow so it's actually used, not forgotten. Dev machine integration: (1) Mount Neon shares on WSL — Samba mount in /etc/fstab or systemd automount so /mnt/neon/hexworth is always available. (2) Database connection profiles — set up .pgpass and mongosh connection strings on dev machines for quick DB access. (3) VS Code Remote-SSH — configure VS Code to connect to Neon for editing files directly on server when needed. (4) Git workflow — option A: continue developing locally, push to GitHub, Neon pulls from GitHub (webhook or cron). Option B: develop on Neon via SSH/Remote, push to GitHub from Neon. Option C: local dev + Neon as CI/staging (git push triggers Neon deploy). (5) Repo Scout integration — configure _tools/repo-scout to write discoveries to Neon's database instead of local JSON. (6) Content pipeline — raw source content (PPTX, PDF from EHE, forked repos) stored on Neon's bulk storage, accessed from dev machines via network share. (7) Firebase sync — option to run Firebase CLI from Neon for deployments (firebase deploy from server). (8) Alias/shortcut setup — add ssh aliases and shell functions to .bashrc on dev machines for quick Neon access (ssh neon, neon-db, neon-logs).

sprints.title: User Messaging System — DMs, Inbox, Purge Rules & Moderation
sprints.notes:
Platform-wide user-to-user messaging system. This is the parent epic — see F-23A through F-23F for sub-tasks.

Architecture: Firestore conversation threads pattern. conversations/{convoId} doc (participants[], lastMessage, updatedAt, unreadCount per user) with messages subcollection (sender, text, timestamp, read). This avoids flat message collection query costs and scales well for inbox rendering.

Purge policy: TTL-based (messages auto-delete after 90 days) + cap-based (max 100 messages per conversation, oldest trimmed). Scheduled Cloud Function runs daily purge.

Moderation: This is a B2B educational platform with students. Messaging must have safeguards — handler/instructor visibility option per class, report button, ability to disable messaging per account. This is a policy decision that must be resolved before launch.

Integration points: UserProfileModal (Send Message button), dashboard header (unread badge), FirestoreManager (new methods), firestore.rules (new collections).

Estimate: 3-5x effort of UserProfileModal. Largest feature build to date.

sprints.title: 2-Player Mode for Arcade Games
sprints.notes: Add 2-player options to arcade games. Modes to consider: (1) Split-screen local — two players on same device with split keyboard controls (WASD + arrows). (2) Turn-based — players alternate rounds and compare scores. (3) Real-time multiplayer via Firestore — shared game state, each player sees the other's position/score live. (4) Ghost mode — play against a recorded run from another player. Start with split-screen local or turn-based as MVP since they require no backend changes. Games to target first: Cloud Hop (competitive platforming — who climbs higher), SQL Injection Defense (competitive — who scores higher in same rounds), Don't series games (turn-based score comparison). UI: mode select on start screen (1P / 2P), player indicators, dual score display, winner announcement. Consider: GameTracker integration for 2P stats, leaderboard entries for 2P matches, achievements for multiplayer wins.

sprints.title: Explore Multiplayer Mode for The Hive
sprints.notes: Explore and design multiplayer capabilities for The Hive dungeon crawler. Currently single-player only (solo room navigation, puzzles, Red Queen AI). Multiplayer concepts to explore: (1) Co-op Exploration — 2-4 players navigate the facility together in real-time via Firestore, see each other's positions on the SVG map, collaborate on puzzles, split up to cover more ground. (2) Competitive Speedrun — players race through the same floor simultaneously, first to solve all puzzles wins, ghost positions visible on map. (3) Asymmetric Mode — one player controls the Red Queen (sets traps, locks doors, chooses dialogue) while others explore, turning PvE into PvP. (4) Party System — lobby/invite system, shared session codes, voice/text chat integration. (5) Cooperative Puzzles — puzzles that require multiple players to solve simultaneously (one player sees clues the other needs). Technical: Firestore real-time listeners for player positions and game state, session documents with player roster, conflict resolution for shared puzzle state, latency handling for room transitions. Current architecture: HiveEngine.js manages state, MapRenderer.js draws SVG, RoomRenderer.js handles UI — would need multiplayer state layer on top. Ties into F-23 (messaging) and F-21 (profiles) for player identity.

sprints.title: AI Art Pipeline — FAL-Generated Game Assets (Debugger Pilot)
sprints.notes: Establish a FAL (fal.ai) image generation pipeline to produce high-quality game art assets, replacing hand-coded canvas pixel art. Pilot game: shield-debugger.applet.html (F-44 Doom-style FPS) — chosen because raycasting engines live or die by texture quality and enemy sprite variety. PHASE 1 — DEBUGGER PILOT ASSETS: (1) Wall textures — 64x64 or 128x128 tileable textures for each system layer: Userspace (clean server room tiles, fluorescent lighting), Network Stack (cable conduit walls, blinking LEDs), Kernel (raw circuit board traces, capacitor arrays), Firmware (dark metallic plating, warning stripes). Need floor/ceiling textures too. (2) Enemy sprites — each enemy type needs front-facing sprite at minimum, ideally 4-8 angle views for raycasting rotation: Buffer Overflow (bloated glitching mass), Trojan (disguised friendly process + revealed hostile form), Worm (segmented snake-like, multiply animation), Ransomware (padlock-headed enforcer), Zero-Day (glitch/stealth shimmer). Death/pain animation frames for each. (3) Weapon sprites — first-person view-model sprites for each weapon: Firewall Shotgun, Antivirus Rifle, Packet Sniffer Scanner, Sandbox Grenade, IDS Turret, Full Format BFG. Need idle + fire + reload frames. (4) HUD elements — health bar frame, ammo counter, minimap border, threat scanner overlay, pickup item sprites (ammo boxes, health kits = system patches, armor = encryption). sprints.title: Messaging — Firestore Data Model & Security Rules
sprints.notes:
Design and implement the Firestore data model for messaging.

Collections:
- conversations/{convoId} — participants[] (2 UIDs), lastMessage (preview text), lastMessageAt (timestamp), unreadCount (map: {uid1: N, uid2: N}), createdAt
- conversations/{convoId}/messages/{msgId} — sender (UID), text (string), timestamp, read (boolean)

Security rules:
- Users can only read/write conversations where their UID is in participants[]
- Messages: sender must match auth.uid on create
- No client delete (only Cloud Functions can purge)
- Rate limit: Cloud Function validates max N messages per hour per user

Indexes:
- conversations: composite index on participants + lastMessageAt (for inbox query)
- messages: timestamp ascending (for chronological thread view)

This is the foundation — all other sub-tasks depend on it.

sprints.title: Messaging — Cloud Functions (send, purge, rate-limit)

3. Rate limiting: max 30 messages per hour per user. Track in users/{uid}/message_rate_limits subcollection (same pattern as flag_attempts).
